sections.title: One claim format. Every payer in India.
sections.subtitle: The National Health Claim Exchange connects every hospital, insurer, TPA and government scheme on one protocol, so claims move as structured data, settle in days instead of months, and cost far less to process. Build and certify in the sandbox, free.

sections.title: Built for every actor in the claims network
From the hospital's HMIS to auto-adjudication at the payer
sections.intro: A claim leaves the hospital as machine-readable FHIR (coded diagnoses, itemised bills, verified identity), so the payer's engine can price and decide it without a human re-keying anything.
sections.sourceNote: Discharge summary, bill lines and codes leave the HMIS as a signed FHIR bundle: no PDFs, no re-typing.
sections.hubNote: Schema-checked and signed in transit, with an immutable trail on both sides.
sections.targetNote: Rules run against clean data, so routine claims clear straight through and only exceptions reach a reviewer.

sections.title: Structured health records pay off on both sides of the claim
sections.intro: A scanned discharge summary is a document someone has to read. The same record as a FHIR bundle is data a system can price, check and settle. That single difference is what changes the economics of a claim for the hospital and for the payer alike.

cards.title: Cash cycle shortens

cards.title: No document chase
cards.description: Codes, bill lines and supporting records travel with the claim, so far fewer queries and resubmissions come back.

cards.title: One integration, every payer
cards.description: The HMIS speaks the protocol once instead of maintaining a portal workflow per insurer and scheme.

cards.title: Fewer avoidable rejections
cards.description: Validation happens at submission, not weeks later: errors surface while the claim is still fixable.

cards.title: Straight-through processing
cards.description: Coded diagnoses and itemised charges let rules engines price routine claims without a human touching them.

cards.title: Fraud and abuse caught early
cards.description: Signed, de-duplicated, traceable exchanges make upcoding, repeat billing and impossible combinations visible.

cards.title: Lower cost per claim
cards.description: Adjudicators spend their time on genuine exceptions instead of re-keying data from PDFs.

cards.title: Analytics that hold up
cards.description: Consistent codes across every provider make utilisation, package pricing and network performance comparable.

items.question: Who should onboard to the sandbox?
items.answer: Any hospital, insurer, TPA, government scheme or software vendor building health-claim exchange capability. The sandbox exists so each participant can test its own components against the communication standards and get certified before touching production.

items.question: What happens after I submit the application?
items.answer: Applications are verified against the details in the form: a semi-manual step, so expect review latency rather than instant provisioning. Duplicate requests from one participant, participants not registered with any registry, TSPs without a valid website and spam are filtered out. Approved participants are added to the sandbox and issued credentials; follow your application on the Status page.

items.question: Which registry ID do I use?
items.answer: Providers use the HFR ID generated during ABDM integration. Payers and TPAs use the IRDAI (or respective authority) ID with leading zeros stripped: 0123 is passed as 123. End-user applications may use their client ID. An entity can hold several participant IDs, one per linked HFR ID.

items.question: What are the role and registry codes, and do they differ between sandbox and production?
items.answer: They are the same in both. Roles: PROVIDER 10001, PAYER 10002, AGENCY_TPA 10003, EUA 10009. Registries: HFR/EUA 10001, PAYER/TPA 10004. Note that 10001 means PROVIDER as a role and HFR/EUA as a registry: different enums in different fields. Wrong mapping causes access issues, rejections or misrouting.

items.question: Can I test without a real payer or provider partner?
items.answer: Yes. The sandbox provides a dummy payer, participant 1000003538@hcx, for insurance plan, coverage eligibility, pre-auth, claim, payment notice and communication. You drive its answer yourself (Approve, Reject or Query) through a control endpoint that does not exist in production, so remove it from your code before go-live.

items.question: How do I get a session token, and how long does it last?
items.answer: Exchange the client_id and client_secret issued at onboarding for a bearer token with an OAuth 2.0 client-credentials call to /get/session. The token lives 1200 seconds (20 minutes): cache it, refresh it well inside that window and never log it. Sandbox tokens do not work against production and vice versa.

items.question: Why do I get 401 Unauthorized?
items.answer: Three usual causes: the token was sent without the Bearer prefix; it has expired: “Sender is not authorized to execute the operation” is the expiry message, so renew via the session API; or it was minted for the other environment. On a 401 discard the cached token, mint a new one and replay once; a second 401 means the credentials themselves are wrong.

items.question: How is the payload protected on the wire?
items.answer: Every request body is a JWE in compact serialization: RSA-OAEP-256 wraps the content key with the recipient’s public certificate and A256GCM encrypts the FHIR bundle. The x-hcx-* routing headers sit in the protected header, so the gateway routes without reading clinical content: the payload is unreadable even to NHCX.

items.question: Where does the recipient’s certificate come from, and do I sign the payload as well?
items.answer: Fetch it from the registry with /fetch/certs and cache it for 24 hours. No separate signature is needed: JWE’s authenticated encryption (AEAD) already protects the integrity of the ciphertext and the protected header. Rotate your own encryption key yearly and report any compromise at once.

items.question: Is any transaction synchronous?
items.answer: No. The gateway never returns a business decision on the same connection. A submission is acknowledged with HTTP 202 and the answer arrives later as a separate inbound call to your on_ endpoint: /preauth/submit is answered on /preauth/on_submit. Every participant is therefore also an HTTP server.

items.question: What must my callback endpoint return?
items.answer: HTTP 202 Accepted with the acceptance body, within 30 seconds. Anything else (a 200, a malformed body, an adjudication holding the socket) is treated as an error: the gateway retries the same message up to five times and then deletes the correlation ID. Acknowledge first, adjudicate after, and be idempotent on x-hcx-correlation_id.

items.question: My callback never arrives. What do I check?
items.answer: In order: the callback URL uses a domain name, not an IP address or port; the server is India-based; the NHCX NAT addresses 3.109.99.210, 13.126.152.0 and 13.200.129.223 are whitelisted; the firewall is not dropping them; and the request is not being misrouted inside your own gateway or load balancer.

items.question: What is the v1/error API, and do I have to implement it?
items.answer: Yes, every integrator must. It is the sender-side endpoint that receives reject details when a message never reached its recipient or the recipient failed to handle it. Without it a request that died at the gateway looks, from the hospital desk, identical to one still under review.

items.question: What is the difference between api_call_id, request_id and correlation_id?
items.answer: All three are 36-character UUIDs. x-hcx-api_call_id is new on every single call; x-hcx-request_id is new per request payload; x-hcx-correlation_id is constant for the whole conversation and is what responders copy back, so persist it against your case before you post. After five failed deliveries the correlation ID is dead: start a fresh cycle with a new one.

items.question: Which timestamp format does x-hcx-timestamp take?
items.answer: The published sources disagree: the PMJAY handbook shows an IST ISO-8601 value (2026-03-19T11:46:34+05:30) and warns that other zones fail validation, while the integrator FAQ gives a zero-UTC form (2024-05-20T11:29:27.358Z). Validate against the environment you are integrating with rather than assuming; the documentation records both.

items.question: Which recipient code do I put in the header?
items.answer: The registry participant code, namespaced as code@hcx. For a payer take the processingID from the get/policies response, not the PayerID field, which is one of the most common integration mistakes. Your own code goes in x-hcx-sender_code.

items.question: What is the difference between NHCX-* and PAYR-* error codes?
items.answer: NHCX-* codes are raised by the exchange gateway: the headers, registration or transport are wrong and the payer never saw the request. PAYR-* codes come from the payer side, either the bridge that validates FHIR or the adjudication engine. PAYR numbers are reused across sheets with different meanings, so match on the description string and log both.

items.question: What does NHCX-1006 “Duplicate request” mean?
items.answer: A message with the same correlation ID already exists in the gateway. Correlation IDs are unique per request cycle: reuse one (including after a failed cycle) and the gateway rejects it. Mint a new UUID and resubmit.

items.question: What does certification actually get me?
items.answer: A successful-completion certificate from the sandbox, valid for a configured period, issued after your functional and security test results are reviewed. That certificate is what the production onboarding review asks for; depending on policy the sandbox may also require STQC or CERT-IN review.

items.question: What is tested at sandbox exit?
items.answer: A fixed use-case list: 13 for providers (registry lookups, session, eligibility, insurance plan, pre-auth, communication, claim, search, payment-notice acknowledgement, task, status) and 15 for payers. Every payload must validate against the NRCeS profiles, responses must carry the right correlation and receiver codes, and rejections use a ProtocolResponse.

items.question: What changes when I go live?
items.answer: The gateway base URL, the credentials, the certificates you encrypt against (re-fetch from production) and the counterparty: the dummy payer, its control endpoints and the test provider and policy IDs must be removed. Bundles, headers and encryption stay the same. PMJAY–NHCX is a separate track with extra scheme configuration.

apply.title: Apply for access to the NHCX sandbox
apply.intro: Tell us who you are, which role you will play on the exchange and what you want to test. Applications are reviewed by the onboarding desk; you will receive an application ID immediately and can track it on the status page.
apply.documentsNote: Attach the registration certificate for a company, LLP or firm (CIN or LLPIN) or PAN and address proof for an individual or proprietorship. PDF, PNG or JPG, up to 10 MB each.
apply.consentText: I confirm that the details above are accurate, that I am authorised to apply on behalf of the organisation named, and I agree to the sandbox terms of use and privacy policy below.
apply.successText: Keep this application ID safe: together with the email address you used, it lets you track the review on the status page. The onboarding desk typically responds within two working days.
apply.errorText: The application could not be submitted because the exchange's content service is not reachable right now. Nothing was sent. Please try again in a few minutes; if the problem persists, write to the onboarding desk with the details you entered.
apply.privacyText: The details you submit are used only to assess and process your sandbox access application and to contact you about it. They are stored by the National Health Authority's sandbox onboarding desk, are not shared with third parties, and are removed when the application is withdrawn or the sandbox account is closed. Uploaded documents are visible only to reviewers.
apply.termsText: The NHCX sandbox is a test environment. It holds no real beneficiary, policy or claim data and must not be sent any. Access is granted to named participants for integration and certification, may be revoked for misuse, and carries no service-level commitment. Passing the sandbox exit checklist is a prerequisite for, not a guarantee of, production onboarding.
